items.title: Native American depopulation, reforestation, and fire regimes in the Southwest United States, 1492–1900 CE
items.who: M. J. Liebmann, J. Farella, C. I. Roos et al.
items.note: Dates Pueblo depopulation in the Jemez Mountains with tree rings and links it to forest regrowth and fire, a regional test of contact-era decline.

items.title: A time transect of exomes from a Native American population before and after European contact
items.who: J. Lindo, E. Huerta-Sánchez, S. Nakagome et al.
items.note: Ancient and modern exomes from the Prince Rupert Harbour region model a post-contact population contraction of roughly 57 percent.

items.title: Pre-Columbian earth-builders settled along the entire southern rim of the Amazon
items.who: J. G. de Souza, D. P. Schaan, M. Robinson et al.
items.note: Survey of fortified villages and earthworks in the upper Tapajós, with a model suggesting up to about a million people in the southern-rim belt.

items.title: Ancient lowland Maya complexity as revealed by airborne laser scanning of northern Guatemala
items.who: M. A. Canuto, F. Estrada-Belli, T. G. Garrison et al.
items.note: PACUNAM lidar over 2,144 km² yields Late Classic population estimates of 7 to 11 million for the lowlands, a reminder of how much earlier densities exceeded contact-era ones.

items.title: Earth system impacts of European colonization of the Americas
items.note: Released compilation of 119 regional population estimates and land-use parameters underlying the Koch et al. hemispheric reconstruction.

items.title: Earth System Impacts of the European Arrival and Great Dying in the Americas after 1492
items.who: A. Koch, C. Brierley, M. M. Maslin and S. L. Lewis
items.note: Meta-analysis giving about 60.5 million for 1492 (IQR 44.8–78.2 million) and roughly 90 percent mortality by 1600, tied to a CO2 drop.

items.title: Spatiotemporal patterns of pre-Columbian people in Amazonia
items.who: C. N. H. McMichael and M. B. Bush
items.note: Distribution models built on radiocarbon-dated sites place late pre-contact Amazonian populations mainly in peripheral and riverine zones rather than across the interior.

items.title: A genetic history of the pre-contact Caribbean
items.who: D. M. Fernandes, K. A. Sirak, H. Ringbauer et al.
items.note: Genomes of 174 individuals; shared-segment analysis implies Caribbean populations in the low tens of thousands, far below chroniclers' millions for Hispaniola.

items.title: Non-uniform tropical forest responses to the 'Columbian Exchange' in the Neotropics and Asia-Pacific
items.who: R. Hamilton, J. Wolfhagen, N. Amano et al.
items.note: Palaeoecological records show no consistent forest regrowth after contact, questioning reforestation-based inferences about the scale of depopulation.

items.title: p3k14c, a synthetic global database of archaeological radiocarbon dates
items.who: D. Bird, L. Miranda, M. Vander Linden et al.
items.note: Open compilation of over 180,000 dates, heavily weighted to the Americas, used for summed-probability population proxies before contact.

items.title: Lidar reveals pre-Hispanic low-density urbanism in the Bolivian Amazon
items.who: H. Prümers, C. Jaimes Betancourt, J. Iriarte et al.
items.note: Lidar maps Casarabe-culture settlement networks in the Llanos de Mojos, supporting larger Amazonian populations, though the culture predates 1492.

items.title: More than 10,000 pre-Columbian earthworks are still hidden throughout Amazonia
items.who: V. Peripato, C. Levis, G. A. Moreira et al.
items.note: Lidar transects and a predictive model estimate 10,000 to 24,000 undiscovered earthworks, implying a larger and more widespread pre-contact Amazonian population.

items.title: Two thousand years of garden urbanism in the Upper Amazon
items.who: S. Rostain, A. Dorison, G. de Saulieu et al.
items.note: Lidar of the Upano Valley, Ecuador, reveals dense platform settlements and roads occupied c. 500 BCE to 300–600 CE, abandoned well before contact.

items.title: Spatiotemporal distribution of the North American Indigenous population prior to European contact
items.who: R. L. Kelly, M. Mackie, S. Pelton and E. Robinson
items.note: Uses over 61,000 radiocarbon dates to model a continental peak around 1150 CE and substantial decline before 1492, lowering the contact baseline for the United States.
